Simas PraÅ¡mantas, LRT.lt 2026.08.25 08:00 Russian troops meet Vladimir Putin. | AP Growing fears about a potential attack against the Baltic states or Poland benefit Russia, which seeks to reduce Western support for Ukraine, Baltic experts told LRT.lt. In early August, Lithuanian Defence Minister Robert Kaunas warned that Russia was considering possible provocations in the Baltic region, including so-called false-flag operations targeting the regionâs critical infrastructure using Ukrainian drones and blaming Kyiv for the attacks. Polandâs Foreign Minister RadosÅaw Sikorski has repeatedly warned of an identical scenario in his country. The warnings should be viewed in the broader context of Russiaâs efforts to reduce Western support for Ukraine, according to Erkki Tori, Director of the National Security and Defence Coordination at the Estonian Government Office. âSince the beginning of this year, the Russians have been looking for ways to tip the balance back in their favour. One of the things they have been working on â and they have been trying to do this since 2022 â is reducing Western support for Ukraine,â Tori told LRT.lt. In his assessment, the Russian threat should not be understood simply as a conflict between Moscow and the Baltic states. âIt is actually Russia against the West as a whole. Russia against NATO, Russia against the European Union, because the goal is to divide us so that we are not as determined to continue supporting Ukraine,â the Estonian official said. Preparing for the unexpected NATO has reportedly drawn up detailed plans for countering missile attacks, stopping Russian forces at the border and disrupting supply routes deep inside Russian territory. The latest warnings also do not indicate a change in the overall security outlook, according to Marek Kohv, head of the Security and Resilience Programme at the International Centre for Defence and Security (ICDS) in Estonia. âI think there is actually nothing new in these warnings, and people sometimes overestimate the new assessments, saying that Russia might do something in the hybrid sphere. But we have to realise that Russia has already been attacking us for years in the hybrid domain, so there is nothing new,â Kohv told LRT.lt. Russia's attacks against Ukraine. | AP Cyberattacks against critical infrastructure have already become a persistent problem in Europe, he added. According to Kohv, Moscow benefits from amplifying fear of possible escalation in Western societies, meaning that the new warnings ultimately work to Russiaâs advantage. US intelligence warnings are taken seriously in Estonia, but the countryâs national security assessment has not changed. âAll the possibilities described in those assessments are relevant today. Russia could use Ukrainian drones if it has them. But from our perspective, the security assessment has not changed since the beginning of the year. At the moment, we [in Estonia] do not have the same concerns that Lithuania or Poland have publicly expressed,â he said. Moscow could intensify information operations, especially ahead of upcoming elections, Kohv said. âI think we will see intensifying disinformation campaigns, particularly against Latvia and, next year, against Estonia as well, because we have elections coming up. Russia has always regarded elections as one of its targets in an effort to change the political situation,â he added. Estonian intelligence continues to assess that conventional military operations against the Baltic states are unlikely as long as Russian forces remain focused on the war in Ukraine. âInstead, we are primarily thinking about various forms of hybrid activity: sabotage, cyberattacks or information campaigns,â said Tori from the Estonian Governmentâs Office. âYou cannot rule out a miscalculation from Russia. This is a lesson that we in the Baltic and Nordic countries have already learned,â he added. A threat that has existed for decades The threat from Moscow has existed since1995, which was when Soviet troops withdrew from their territory and returned to Russia, according to Sandis Å raders, a researcher at the Latvian Institute of International Affairs (LIIA) and the National Defence Academy of Latvia. âRussian bases are close to the Latvian and Estonian borders. We have a direct border with the Russian Federation. In Lithuaniaâs case, Kaliningrad is a heavily militarised region, so the threat has always existed,â he told LRT.lt. Å raders stresses that Russia had been projecting aggressive military capabilities towards the Baltic region long before its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Since the invasion began, manifestations of Russian aggression in the Baltic states â airspace violations, military exercises and attacks on critical infrastructure â have become increasingly brazen. âIn the Baltic states, violations of our airspace have already become a routine occurrence, something both the public and military structures are almost becoming bored of â all those instances when fighter jets have to be scrambled from the Å iauliai Air Base or, for example, from Ãmari Air Base in Estonia,â Å raders said. Following Russiaâs aggression against Ukraine in 2014, the Baltic states are also aware of the so-called âlittle green menâ scenario. âWe know that similar military exercises and incidents have also been recorded along the Estonian border, for example near Narva,â Å raders notes. Speaking about warnings of a possible Russian false-flag operation involving Ukrainian drones, the Latvian defence expert says he feels safer knowing that intelligence officials are already aware of such plans by Moscow. Drones in Russian-Belarusian military drills | AP Weakened Putin needs a win? Warnings about possible Russian provocations in the Baltic states and Poland have intensified as Russia faces growing pressure in Ukraine. Kyivâs attacks in Russia itself represent a significant blow not only to Russiaâs economy and military logistics, but also to President Vladimir Putinâs domestic image. Some observers believe that this could prompt the Kremlin leader to seek victories elsewhere and undertake an operation on NATOâs eastern flank designed to test the allianceâs unity. âIn such a case, Russia could test NATOâs resolve â whether our response plans are in place and whether national military structures are prepared for provocations and false-flag military operations,â Å raders said. âThere will always be people in Baltic societies who will say that if a Ukrainian drone flies into Latvia, Estonia or Lithuania, it is Ukraineâs fault. Therefore, we have to look very carefully at the combination of different types of operations and at NATOâs resolve. âUnfortunately, the Baltic states, as smaller members of NATO and the European Union, are more vulnerable than, for example, Finland or Poland,â he added. Kohv from ICDS in Estonia believes that an attack against the Baltic states or Poland would produce the opposite result from what the Kremlin would want. âI do not see how Putin could reduce the pressure Ukraine is putting on Russia by attacking the Baltic states or Poland. I think it would only further unite Europe in supporting Ukraine and taking action against various Russian capabilities or assets that it has here,â he said. According to Kohv, Moscowâs hybrid operations have already changed the way some European countries view their own security. As an example, he points to the August 5 incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany, where a drone carrying explosives was found near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft. Following the incident, the German government granted intelligence agencies broader powers to counter hybrid threats and take active defensive measures. âIn our region, it has always been understood that Russia is capable of various actions. I hope Western Europe will now wake up as well,â Kohv says. LRT English Newsletter Every Friday morning. Thanks for subscribing! I will be your ride or die in Trump World.” In the texts, Guilfoyle gave Deters pointers on how to help her without leaving a paper trail, informing him that the payment “won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express.” In an interview with the Journal, Deters said that he ultimately didn’t send Guilfoyle the money, as she’d made promises of favors to him in the past without ever delivering. Among other things, the former Trump donor explained, he once offered to pay Guilfoyle $1 million in exchange for securing him an interview on Tucker Carlson’s show. While Guilfoyle said she could get Carlson to agree to the interview, she was unable to convince him. “She never came through on anything,” Deters explained. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio , who is currently in Greece, refused to comment on the corruption allegations when asked by reporters on Thursday. “Our job is not to respond every time somebody gives the media something without any advanced warning, without any chance to look at it,” Rubio said. “That’s not the way you run an organization, and that’s not a serious way to conduct the policy of our country. So I’m not going to comment on a story that literally posted a few hours ago.” Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Va.), a member of the House Oversight Committee, wrote in a Wednesday social media post that Guilfoyle’s efforts to hide elicit transactions was doomed to failure. “The Trump cartel can’t hide this,” Walkinshaw wrote . “Corruption leaves a paper trail. It’s time to Investigate every message and dollar.” Democracy Defenders Action co-founder Norm Eisen, who served as US ambassador to the Czech Republic under President Barack Obama , expressed astonishment at the Guilfoyle texts. “I was an ambassador myself and I’ve never seen anything like this,” Eisen wrote . “She denies it, but you can smell this one from Athens!” Blog Archive ▼ 2026 (1916) ▼ October (149) Sen. The chapter traces its roots to 2015, when fewer than 10 local residents met at the library to reestablish an SAR presence in the region. The new chapter's officers were Jonathan Guerrier, John Opre, Phil Bracy and John Layfield. Their efforts led to official certification in 2016 and the formation of the Mahoning Valley Chapter. The Mahoning Valley Chapter now serves the same three counties: Mahoning, Trumbull and Columbiana. Among the Chapter's most notable recent achievements was dedicating a monument in downtown East Liverpool honoring all Revolutionary War veterans buried in Columbiana County. The project was led by past president Stephen Barlow through a community fundraising campaign. The chapter continues its mission to promote historical education, honor the nation's founding principles and serve the community through patriotism and civic engagement. During the Oct. 3 meeting, President Wayne Recknor welcomed guest speaker Suzie McCabe of the Canfield Historical Society. McCabe presented a program on Revolutionary War veterans buried in Canfield and ongoing efforts to preserve and research local historic cemeteries. Members elected Richard "Dick" Altomare as vice president. Service pins were presented to Recknor for five years of service and Jonathan Guerrier for 10 years of service. The meeting concluded with a Revolutionary War history reading by John Opre, who discussed the military events of October 1776 and the contributions of Polish military engineer Thaddeus Kosciuszko. The chapter's next meeting and Christmas gathering will be Dec. 12 at Davidson's Restaurant in Canfield. Interested individuals are welcome to attend. Starting at /week. Subscribe Today

https://bnn-news.com/lithuania/lithuania.text: Photo: Magnific Advertisements The smuggling of counterfeit tobacco products from Latvia into Lithuania is increasing after authorities stepped up efforts to curb cigarette smuggling from Belarus using weather balloons, Donatas Škarnulis, acting head of Lithuania's State Border Guard Service, announced on Monday. "The overall shift in trends shows that the share of tobacco smuggling from Belarus is declining. Looking at developments over several years, counterfeit tobacco products from Latvia are now becoming dominant, with a larger proportion coming from Latvia than from Belarus," Škarnulis told Lithuanian public broadcaster LRT. Škarnulis said that efforts to combat smuggling using weather balloons have been effective. "Last year, approximately 200 people were held accountable in cases involving balloons alone. This year, we also have dozens of cases. This is our ongoing work, and it is certainly producing results," the acting border guard chief said. Advertisements "This year alone, the number of shipments transported by balloons is three times lower than last year, while the quantity of tobacco products brought in this way has fallen by approximately half," he added. According to Škarnulis, these results have been achieved through preventive measures carried out by border guards, police and customs officers, as well as criminal intelligence operations and pre-trial investigations conducted by the State Border Guard Service and police. Data published by Lithuania's State Border Guard Service last week show that Lithuanian authorities have intercepted 182 shipments of smuggled cigarettes transported from Belarus by weather balloons so far this year. By comparison, 635 such shipments were intercepted last year, while 226 were recorded in 2024. Border guards have also brought down 67 smuggling drones carrying illegal tobacco shipments from Belarus into Lithuania this year. Advertisements Last year, 59 such drones were intercepted, compared with 54 in 2024. Lithuania has introduced a range of measures to combat smuggling, including declaring a national-level emergency and conducting law enforcement operations. These operations have also uncovered suspicions that border guards and police officers may have been involved in smuggling activities. Lithuanian leaders regard the airspace violations caused by smuggling balloons as a hybrid attack by the Minsk regime.
